output.headline: Carers and drivers set for relief as Healey delivers first budget
output.standfirst: Healey is set to scrap the carers’ allowance cliff edge and cancel January’s fuel duty rise in his first budget, even as bigger decisions on tax, defence and welfare are deferred amid a strained economy.
output.bodyHtml:
John Healey will strike an optimistic note in his first budget on Wednesday, signalling “fresh hope for the future” and giving households breathing space from rising cost of living pressures, despite a turbulent international backdrop.

Healey insists he will put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget, acknowledging that the UK faces a “difficult moment” against a turbulent global economic backdrop.

The budget will be read as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, though it is expected to be a relatively modest affair, with Healey putting off bigger decisions on tax and spending until next year amid stark fiscal realities.

“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”

Related: Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor

Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families ahead of a steep rise in typical energy bills in January, while pledging energy market reforms to bring bills down for all households in the longer term.

Andy Burnham has told MPs he is keen to abolish the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – a move that would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, with the cost picked up by those who use more.

As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected to end the carers’ allowance cliff edge – which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit by as little as a few pence a week – and to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.

Healey will announce plans to raise the minimum wage by nearly 4%, though he will slow the increase for under-21s after warnings that they were being priced out of jobs – a decision that has prompted accusations that Labour has broken a manifesto pledge.

He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for retirement, shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax, and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost for middle earners.

Healey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.

Cost-of-living measures are set to feature heavily in the budget, even though the chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil from the Iran conflict.

In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”

Industry experts fear that further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture will bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.

The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.

Healey is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – though he will wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.

The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.

But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.

Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.

Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.

The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.

City analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.

The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.

At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.

Consumer confidence has fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.

Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”

Related: You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

To help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised to raise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.

The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.

The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”

The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”
output.progress: Healey is also raising the minimum wage, shielding pensioners from income tax, and raising the bank surcharge to help offset the economic damage from the Middle East war.
